blocks.content: The previous topic named the three relationship shapes, one to one, one to many, and many to many, an ER diagram, entity relationship diagram, is the visual tool used to actually map those relationships out across an entire schema before writing a single CREATE TABLE statement.

This topic covers the core building blocks of an ER diagram, entities, attributes, and relationships, the standard notation used to mark relationship cardinality, and why sketching this out first tends to save real rework later.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438608357-390329499.png
1. What an Entity Represents
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438608357-525989100.png

An entity in an ER diagram represents one table, drawn as a labeled box, Customer, Order, Product, each entity later becomes a CREATE TABLE statement, the entity name itself typically becomes the table name.
2. What an Attribute Represents

An attribute lists the actual columns that entity will have, id, name, email for a Customer entity, this maps directly onto the columns covered in the earlier Tables, Rows, and Columns topic, sketched out before any SQL is written.
{"headers":["ER Diagram Concept","Maps To"],"rows":[["Entity","A table"],["Attribute","A column on that table"]]}
3. What a Relationship Line Represents
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438609293-760346312.png

A line connecting two entities represents a relationship between them, often labeled with a verb describing that relationship, a Customer places an Order, this line is exactly what becomes a foreign key, covered in an earlier topic, once the schema is actually implemented.
4. Marking Cardinality on the Diagram
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438609295-30981095.png

Cardinality notation, a 1 on one end of the relationship line and an N on the other, marks exactly which relationship shape from the previous topic applies, one Customer connects to N Orders, this small notation detail is what actually specifies one to one, one to many, or many to many on the diagram itself.

blocks.title: Crow foot notation is another common style
blocks.content: Some teams use crow foot symbols, a forked line end, instead of plain 1 and N labels to mark cardinality, the underlying meaning is identical, pick whichever notation your team already recognizes and stay consistent with it.
Common cardinality notations

1 --- 1   one to one
1 --- N   one to many
M --- N   many to many

blocks.content: 5. Representing a Many to Many Relationship
blocks.text: 5. Representing a Many to Many Relationship

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438609296-460873209.png
blocks.alt: Representing a Many to Many Relationship

blocks.content: A many to many relationship on the diagram, Student enrolls in Course marked M to N, is exactly the case that later requires a junction table, covered in the previous Relationships topic, drawing this out explicitly at the diagram stage makes that junction table requirement visible before any table gets built.

6. ER Diagrams as a Collaboration Tool
blocks.text: 6. ER Diagrams as a Collaboration Tool

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438609297-100515654.png
blocks.alt: ER Diagrams as a Collaboration Tool

blocks.content: An ER diagram is genuinely useful as a shared artifact, a non technical stakeholder can look at a diagram of entities and relationships and confirm it matches their understanding of the business far more easily than reviewing raw SQL, catching a misunderstanding here is far cheaper than catching it after tables are built and populated with real data.

blocks.title: The diagram is a plan, not the final schema
blocks.content: An ER diagram intentionally leaves out implementation detail, exact data types, indexes, constraint names, its job is to get the entities and relationships right first, those details get filled in once the diagram is translated into actual CREATE TABLE statements.
7. From Diagram to Actual Tables
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438609297-497820029.png

Once an ER diagram is reviewed and settled, translating it into SQL is fairly mechanical, each entity becomes a table, each attribute becomes a column, each relationship becomes a foreign key, with many to many relationships specifically becoming a junction table.
8. Common Mistakes
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438609298-196636120.png

["Jumping straight into CREATE TABLE statements for a nontrivial schema without sketching relationships out first","Leaving cardinality notation off relationship lines, making the diagram ambiguous about one to many versus many to many","Treating the ER diagram as a finished technical spec rather than a plan meant to be reviewed and revised","Forgetting that a many to many relationship on the diagram needs a junction table once implemented"]
items: Jumping straight into CREATE TABLE statements for a nontrivial schema without sketching relationships out first
Leaving cardinality notation off relationship lines, making the diagram ambiguous about one to many versus many to many
Treating the ER diagram as a finished technical spec rather than a plan meant to be reviewed and revised
Forgetting that a many to many relationship on the diagram needs a junction table once implemented

blocks.content: 9. Key Takeaways

["Entities, attributes, and relationship lines are the three core building blocks of an ER diagram","Cardinality notation, 1 to 1, 1 to N, or M to N, is what actually specifies the relationship shape on the diagram","Reviewing an ER diagram with stakeholders before building tables catches misunderstandings far more cheaply than catching them later","The next topic, Schema Design Basics, pulls entities, keys, and relationships together into a complete, practical schema design process"]
